Chapter 6: The Realities of Commitment in a World of Infinite Options
You know that quiet moment, right after the first spark of attraction fades? When the excitement of new messages and those fun first dates starts to settle... and you’re left with something deeper—or maybe nothing at all? That’s usually where the real work of a relationship kicks in. But let’s be honest—these days, with endless options just a swipe away, the idea of actually committing to one person can feel overwhelming. Maybe even a little unnatural.
Take this guy in his thirties. After months of dating, he really liked the woman he was seeing. Their conversations flowed, and being together just felt comfortable. But every time he considered making things official, this little voice would whisper, “What if there’s someone better out there?” It’s funny—what once felt exciting, all those choices, suddenly made it hard for him to settle down.
And he’s not alone. This isn’t just indecision—it’s a new kind of anxiety. The feeling that your perfect match might be just one more swipe away. That fear of missing out, the same one we get in so many parts of life? It sneaks right into our love lives, too. You’re torn between wanting genuine connection... and wondering what else might be out there.
But here’s where things start to shift. Commitment doesn’t have to feel like you’re giving something up. In fact, it can be a powerful choice. Picture this: there’s a couple who met online, dated for a few months, and then, together, decided to delete their dating apps. It sounds simple, but to them, it was huge. It was their way of saying, “I choose you, out of all the possibilities.” That small act brought them relief—maybe even joy. The constant pressure to keep searching just melted away, replaced by the comfort of building something real together.
So, here’s the key takeaway: commitment isn’t about losing your options. It’s about investing in one person, giving that connection the space and care it needs to grow. Sure, doubts can linger, and the temptation to compare never totally disappears. But most people discover that the rewards—real intimacy, trust, and shared experiences—are so much more satisfying than the fleeting rush of something new.
